title: The Thirsty Crow
moral: Little by little, a wise mind finds a way.
fable: On a hot summer afternoon, a thirsty crow flew over a dusty village looking for water. The ponds were dry and the wells were empty.
At last it spotted a clay pot in a garden. There was a little water at the bottom, but the crow's beak could not reach it.
The clever crow had an idea. It picked up a pebble and dropped it in, and the water rose a tiny bit. Again and again it dropped pebbles, keeping a careful count in its mind.
Little by little the water climbed up. When it finally reached the crow's beak, the crow drank happily and flew away. It had remembered the count and let it grow.

riddle.question: The crow must remember how many pebbles it has dropped, because that number grows with every single drop. What is the one thing it needs to keep track of, and update, as it works?
options: The colour of the pebbles
A growing number the crow remembers and updates
The shape of the pot
The time of day
riddle.explanation: The crow keeps a single growing count in its mind. In Python we call that a variable - a named box that stores a value and can be updated. Every pebble drop is a small update to that count.

conceptReveal.title: Variables: named boxes for values
conceptReveal.summary: A variable gives a name to a piece of information so you can remember it now and change it later.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
pebbles = 0            # the crow starts with none
pebbles = pebbles + 1  # first drop
pebbles = pebbles + 1  # second drop
print(pebbles)         # 2
points: A variable has a name and a value.
Use = to put a value into the box. This is assignment, not 'equals'.
You can read the old value, change it, and store it back.
Values can be numbers (int), text (str), or True/False (bool).

microLesson.headline: One concept, three small ideas
paragraphs: Like the crow, a program stores information in named boxes called variables. water_level = 0 creates a box named water_level holding the value 0.
When the crow drops a pebble, the value changes: water_level = water_level + 1 takes the current value, adds 1, and stores it back. This is why the right side is read first.
Variables can hold different kinds of values: whole numbers like 7 (int), text like "crow" (str), and yes/no like True (bool).
keyPoints: Assignment x = 5 reads the right side first, then stores it in x.
You can update a value: x = x + 1.
Name variables to describe what they store: pebbles, water_level, crow_name.

challenge.title: Fill the pot: track the pebbles
challenge.instruction: The crow drops pebbles into the pot. Use variables to (1) store the crow's name as text, (2) start the water level at zero, (3) drop four pebbles one at a time, and (4) print the final water level. Finish the starter code.
challenge.starterCode:
# 1. Store the crow's name
crow_name = "Kaali"

# 2. Start the water level at zero
water_level = 0

# 3. Drop four pebbles, one at a time
water_level = water_level + 1
water_level = water_level + 1
water_level = water_level + 1
water_level = water_level + 1

# 4. Print how high the water has risen
print(water_level)
challenge.hint: Each drop is one line: water_level = water_level + 1

check.message: The water rose four times, so the final water level should be 4.

project.title: The Village Water Tank
project.brief: Build a small program for the village. A water tank starts with 10 litres. Three of the crow's friends each add 3 litres. Create the variable tank_water, add 3 litres three times, and print the final amount.
project.starterCode:
# The tank starts with 10 litres
tank_water = 10

# Three friends each add 3 litres
tank_water = tank_water + 3
tank_water = tank_water + 3
tank_water = tank_water + 3

print(tank_water)
project.successHint: Expected output: 19

check.message: 10 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 19 litres in the tank.

title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
moral: Dream of the plan, but keep your feet on the ground.
fable: A village milkmaid named Meera balanced a pail of fresh milk on her head and walked carefully toward the market. Every step had to be steady, or the milk would spill.
As she walked, she began to dream. "When I sell this milk I will have money," she thought. "With that money I will buy a basket of eggs, and every egg will hatch a chick."
"My chicks will grow into hens, and each hen will lay more eggs. Count them with me - one, two, three, fifty! Soon I will have a flock of fifty birds to sell for a handsome price."

Meera nodded so eagerly while counting her unborn chicks that the pail slipped from her head and the milk spilled across the road. "Do not count your chicks before they hatch," laughed the village elder.

riddle.question: Meera keeps a running total that grows at every step - milk to money, money to eggs, eggs to chicks, chicks to hens. What is the Python idea that lets her store a number and update it again and again?
options: A variable - a named box holding a value she can change
A single print statement that never changes
A decision with if and else
A fixed number that can never be rewritten
riddle.explanation: Meera's growing total is exactly a variable. She starts with a value, then updates it step by step: coins = coins + 5, chicks = chicks + 1. The named box keeps only the newest value.

conceptReveal.title: Variables: named boxes that grow
conceptReveal.summary: A variable stores one value under a name, and you can update that value as your story unfolds.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
chicks = 2          # Meera starts with two
chicks = chicks + 1  # a chick hatches
chicks = chicks + 1  # another hatches
print(chicks)        # 4
points: A variable has a name and a value.
Use = to put a value into the box. This is assignment, not 'equals'.
Reading the old value, adding, and storing it back is an update.
Updates can grow a value: coins = coins + 5.

microLesson.headline: One box, many updates
paragraphs: Like Meera's count of chicks, a program stores a running total in a named box called a variable. chicks = 2 creates the box and puts 2 inside.
When one more chick hatches, the value changes: chicks = chicks + 1 reads the current value, adds 1, and stores the new total back into the same box.
Repeat the update and the box grows steadily. Start the box with 0 and you can build any total you like - eggs, coins, hens, or pebbles.
keyPoints: Assignment x = 5 reads the right side first, then stores it in x.
You can update a value: x = x + 1.
A variable holds only the newest value you assigned.

challenge.title: Count the chicks
challenge.instruction: Meera starts with 2 chicks. Three of her hens each hatch one more chick. Update the chicks variable three times, then print the final count.
challenge.starterCode:
# Meera starts with two chicks
chicks = 2

# Three hens each hatch one chick
chicks = chicks + 1
chicks = chicks + 1
chicks = chicks + 1

# Print the final count
print(chicks)
challenge.hint: Each hatch is one line: chicks = chicks + 1

project.title: The Market Ledger
project.brief: Meera sells milk from 4 pots, and each pot earns 5 coins. Track her earnings: start coins at 0, add 5 four times, and print the total.
project.starterCode:
# Meera starts with no coins
coins = 0

# Each pot earns 5 coins
coins = coins + 5
coins = coins + 5
coins = coins + 5
coins = coins + 5

print(coins)
project.successHint: Expected output: 20

check.message: 4 pots x 5 coins = 20 coins.

title: The Dog and His Reflection
moral: Be content with what you have; greed can cost you everything.
fable: A hungry dog trotted home carrying a juicy bone it had found beside the river. It gripped the bone tightly, planning to enjoy it in the shade of its favourite tree.
Crossing a narrow wooden bridge, it glanced down at the calm water. There, in the reflection, it saw another dog - one that seemed to be holding an even bigger bone.
"That bone looks bigger than mine," the greedy dog growled. "I want it!" It opened its mouth to bark at the reflection, and in that instant its own bone splashed into the river and sank.
The dog stared as its treasure disappeared and the reflection faded away. It padded home with nothing, having lost a real bone for a shadow it could never keep.

riddle.question: The dog starts with one bone, reaches for a second, and ends with none. The value it was holding changed completely. What does this teach us about the value stored in a variable?
options: A variable can change - a new assignment replaces the old value
A variable can only ever hold text
A variable cannot be read after it is created
A variable always holds the same value forever
riddle.explanation: A variable is a box you can rewrite. The dog's bone count starts at 1, and the greedy mistake turns it to 0 - the same named box now holds a different value. That is what makes variables so powerful, and why we must be careful.

conceptReveal.title: Variables: values that can be rewritten
conceptReveal.summary: The value in a variable is not fixed. Assignment replaces the old value with the new one.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
bones = 1    # found one bone
bones = 0    # dropped it in the river
print(bones) # 0
points: A variable has a name and a value.
Assigning again overwrites the old value.
The value can grow, shrink, or change type.
Reading a variable gives you its newest value.

microLesson.headline: Rewrite the box
paragraphs: A variable is a named box, and the box can be emptied and refilled. bones = 1 puts the value 1 into the box named bones.
When the dog loses the bone, the program writes bones = 0. The old 1 is gone - the same box now holds 0. This overwriting is how a variable changes over time.
You can build on the newest value too: bones = bones + 2 reads whatever is inside, adds 2, and stores the fresh total back.
keyPoints: Assignment x = 5 stores a value; the next x = 8 overwrites it.
You can update a value: x = x + 1.
Only the newest value is remembered - the old one is gone.

challenge.title: Keep or lose the bone
challenge.instruction: The dog finds one bone, then loses it in the river. Assign bones = 1, overwrite it to 0 and print. Later the dog finds two fresh bones, so update bones by adding 2 and print again.
challenge.starterCode:
# The dog finds one bone
bones = 1

# It loses the bone in the river
bones = 0
print(bones)

# Later it finds two fresh bones
bones = bones + 2
print(bones)
challenge.hint: Assignment replaces the old value: bones = 0 overwrites the 1.

check.message: First the value is 0, then the two fresh bones make it 2.

project.title: The Riverbank Counter
project.brief: Help the pond keeper count the fish in the river. Start count at 0, two fish swim in (add 2), one swims away (subtract 1), then three more arrive (add 3). Print the final count.
project.starterCode:
# The pond keeper starts the count at zero
count = 0

# Two fish swim in
count = count + 2

# One swims away
count = count - 1

# Three more arrive
count = count + 3

print(count)
project.successHint: Expected output: 4

title: The Elephant and the Dog
moral: True friendship is a bond that nothing can take away.
fable: A great elephant lived alone near a village. He was gentle but huge, and all the smaller animals kept away from him, leaving him lonely and sad.
One day a tiny stray dog wandered into the village. Seeing the elephant, she trotted up and lay down in his shadow. "May I stay here?" she asked. "The sun is very hot."
The elephant was overjoyed. "Stay as long as you like," he said. From that day the two were inseparable - the dog slept by the elephant's side and the elephant never let the stray dog go hungry.

But a jealous man lured the dog away with sweet food and harmed her. When the elephant found her gone he cried out in grief. A wise old woman found the bones and told the elephant, "Your friend loved you, and your love for her will never be forgotten." The elephant bowed his head and remembered every moment of joy they had shared.

riddle.question: The elephant's feelings change across the story - lonely, then joyful, then deeply sad. A program can track each feeling with a name and a value. What is this idea?
options: A loop that repeats the same action
A decision made with if and else
A variable - a named box that holds a changing state
A list that stores many items in order
riddle.explanation: Each emotion the elephant feels - loneliness, joy, grief - is a state that can be stored in a variable. The variable's value changes as the story moves forward, just like the elephant's mood.

conceptReveal.title: Variables: storing and updating a state
conceptReveal.summary: A variable can represent a changing state - like an emotion, a count, or a yes/no flag - that is updated as events unfold.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
are_friends = False    # elephant is alone
happiness = 1           # very low
are_friends = True      # the dog arrives
happiness = 8           # they are inseparable
points: A variable can store a True / False flag (a boolean) to represent a state.
You can overwrite the old value at any time: are_friends = True.
Multiple variables can describe one situation from different angles.
Reading a variable always gives you the newest value.

microLesson.headline: State that changes with the story
paragraphs: The elephant's loneliness, joy, and grief are states that change as events unfold. Each state can live in a named variable, like happiness or are_friends.
When the dog arrives, the program writes are_friends = True. The old False is overwritten - the same box now reflects a new reality.
You can use several variables together to tell a richer story: one for friendship, one for happiness, one for how many friends there are.
keyPoints: A boolean variable holds True or False: is_friends = True.
You can update any variable at any time with a new assignment.
Multiple named variables together describe a full state.
Reading a variable always returns its most recent value.

challenge.title: Track the elephant's journey
challenge.instruction: The elephant starts alone and sad. The dog arrives and they become friends. Then the dog is lost. Track the elephant's state with two variables: a boolean is_friends (True or False) and a number happiness (low when sad, high when joyful). Finish the starter code.
challenge.starterCode:
# The elephant is alone and unhappy
is_friends = False
happiness = 1

# The dog arrives - update the state
is_friends = True
happiness = 8

# They spend days together
is_friends = True
happiness = 10

# The dog is lost
is_friends = False
happiness = 0
print(happiness)
print(is_friends)
challenge.hint: Assigning again overwrites the old value in the same variable.

check.message: After losing the dog the elephant's happiness drops to 0 and is_friends becomes False.

project.title: The Elephant's Memory
project.brief: The wise woman says the elephant remembers every joyful day with the dog. Track the memories: start days_together at 0, add 3 joyful days, then add 2 more. Print the final count, and the elephant's name as a string.
project.starterCode:
# The wise woman remembers the friendship
name = "Bhola"
days_together = 0

# Three joyful days pass
days_together = days_together + 3

# Two more joyful days
days_together = days_together + 2

print(days_together)
print(name)
project.successHint: Expected output: 5, then Bhola

check.message: 0 + 3 + 2 = 5 days together, and the elephant's name is Bhola.

title: The Blue Jackal
moral: What you truly are cannot be hidden forever.
fable: A scrawny jackal slunk through the village at dusk, hungry and afraid. Every animal chased him away - the dogs barked, the goats kicked, and even the crows pecked at his tail.
Desperate for shelter he crept into a dyer's workshop and fell into a great vat of blue dye. When he clambered out, his entire body was brilliant blue from nose to tail.
The other animals froze in terror. "What creature is this?" they whispered. "Surely a god has come down to us!" They bowed low and offered the blue jackal the best food and a place to rest.

The jackal loved his new life and called himself King of the Animals. But one moonlit night he heard real jackals howling in the distance and answered with a howl of his own. The animals recognised the voice at once. 'He is no god - he is just a jackal!' they cried, and chased him away. The blue faded, and the jackal was alone again.

riddle.question: The jackal looks like a god because he is blue, but he is really just a jackal. What does the blue colour remind us of in Python?
options: A variable whose stored value can be changed
A loop that runs forever
A list that holds many items
A function that returns a result
riddle.explanation: The blue dye is like assigning a new value to a variable. The name stays the same - it is still a jackal - but the value the animals see (blue) has changed. Variables let us swap one value for another.

conceptReveal.title: Variables: swap one value for another
conceptReveal.summary: Assigning a new value to a variable overwrites the old one. The name is constant; the value can change at any time.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
colour = "brown"
colour = "blue"
print(colour)   # blue
points: A variable holds one value at a time.
Assigning again replaces the old value completely.
The variable name stays the same - only the value changes.
You can overwrite a variable as many times as you like.

microLesson.headline: Same name, different value
paragraphs: The jackal's name never changes, but his colour does. In Python, a variable works the same way: the name stays fixed, but the value inside can be swapped out.
First colour = "brown" stores the original colour. Then colour = "blue" overwrites it - the old value is gone and the box holds the new one.
You can chain as many overwrites as you like: colour = "blue", colour = "red", colour = "gold". Only the most recent assignment matters.
keyPoints: colour = "brown" stores a string value.
colour = "blue" overwrites the old value.
Only the newest value is remembered.
The name stays the same across every assignment.

challenge.title: The jackal's changing coat
challenge.instruction: Track the jackal's appearance. Start with colour = "brown", then overwrite it with "blue" and print. He loses the dye and returns to brown, so overwrite colour again and print the final value.
challenge.starterCode:
# The jackal before the dye
colour = "brown"

# He falls into the vat of blue dye
colour = "blue"
print(colour)

# The dye fades overnight
colour = "brown"
print(colour)
challenge.hint: Assigning a new value to colour replaces the old one.

check.message: First the jackal is blue, then the dye fades and he is brown again.

project.title: The Chameleon's Wardrobe
project.brief: A chameleon changes colour three times: start at "green", overwrite to "red", then to "gold". Print the colour after each change so you can see the sequence.
project.starterCode:
# The chameleon's first colour
shade = "green"
print(shade)

# It changes to red
shade = "red"
print(shade)

# Finally it turns gold
shade = "gold"
print(shade)
project.successHint: Expected output: green, red, gold (each on its own line)

check.message: Three overwrites, three prints, three different colours.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
moral: A friend who cannot be trusted must be judged by his choices.
fable: On the banks of a great river lived a monkey and a crocodile who became fast friends. The monkey ate sweet mangoes and always shared them with the crocodile.
One day the crocodile's wife grew greedy. 'Bring me the monkey's heart, I must taste it!' she demanded. Ashamed, the crocodile agreed and offered the monkey a ride across the river.
Midstream, the crocodile confessed his terrible plan. The monkey thought fast and said, 'I left my heart in the tree! Row back and I will fetch it.'
The foolish crocodile rowed back, and the monkey sprang to the safety of the tree. 'A friend must be judged by his choices,' called the monkey, 'and your choice was a dangerous one!'

riddle.question: The monkey must decide whether to trust the crocodile's offer before stepping onto his back. What kind of thinking does the monkey need here?
options: Repeating the same action many times
Choosing one path based on a condition or warning
Remembering a growing count
Looking up a value by name
riddle.explanation: The monkey weighs a condition - is it safe? - and then picks one of two actions. In Python this is an if/else decision, a conditional.

conceptReveal.title: Conditionals: decisions with if / else
conceptReveal.summary: Programs make choices by checking a condition and running one of two blocks of code.
points: if checks a condition that is True or False.
Only one block runs: the if block, or the else block.
Indentation (4 spaces) tells Python which lines belong to each block.
You can add more branches with elif.

microLesson.headline: Three ingredients of a decision
paragraphs: Every decision needs a condition - a question that is either True or False, like 'is the river risky?'.
If the condition is True, Python runs the indented lines under if. Otherwise it runs the lines under else. Only one block ever runs.
Real programs chain decisions with elif ('else if') for more than two branches, like choosing mango, banana, or nothing.
keyPoints: Conditions compare values: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=.
if runs when True; else catches everything else.
Indent the lines inside each block by 4 spaces.

challenge.title: The dangerous crossing
challenge.instruction: The monkey checks the river before crossing. If it is raining, print "Stay in the tree". Otherwise print "Climb on the crocodile". The variable is_raining is already set - write the if/else to decide.
challenge.starterCode:
# The river is dangerous today
is_raining = True

# Decide: stay or cross?
if is_raining:
    print("Stay in the tree")
else:
    print("Climb on the crocodile")
challenge.hint: An if block runs when its condition is True. Here is_raining is True.

check.message: Since it is raining, the monkey stays safely in the tree.

project.title: The Mango Picker
project.brief: Help the monkey pick ripe mangoes. If a mango's ripeness is 8 or more, print "Ripe mango". Otherwise print "Not ripe yet". Try changing ripeness to test both branches.
project.successHint: Expected output: Ripe mango

check.message: 9 is greater than or equal to 8, so the mango is ripe.

title: The Heron and the Crab
moral: Believe what you see, not only what you are told.
fable: A wise old heron lived beside a quiet pond full of fish and one slow, careful crab. The heron was too old to catch fish by speed, so he thought of a trick.
'Dear friends,' he said one morning, 'I have heard that a hunter is coming to drain the pond. I know a secret pond high in the hills where you will be safe. I will carry you there one by one.'
The fish trusted the heron and climbed onto his beak. One by one he flew to the secret pond - which was not a pond at all, but the top of a tall tree where he ate every last fish.

The crab watched the fish leave and never return. 'Carry me too,' he said, climbing onto the heron's back. Halfway up the crab saw the bones of his friends scattered below. 'You are no saviour,' he said, and snapped the heron's neck with his strong claws. Then he crawled safely back to the pond.

riddle.question: The crab notices that every fish who left with the heron has disappeared. He sees the bones below and must decide instantly: trust the heron or fight back. What is the crab really doing?
options: Repeating one action over and over
Checking a condition and choosing a response
Counting the fish in the pond
Storing a name in a variable
riddle.explanation: The crab gathers information - fish missing, bones visible - and uses it to decide: if the heron is lying, fight back; otherwise, trust him. Checking a condition and acting on it is exactly what an if/else statement does.

conceptReveal.title: Conditionals: decide based on evidence
conceptReveal.summary: An if/else statement lets a program look at the facts and choose a path. True goes one way, False goes the other.
points: A condition is a question: bones_visible == True or fish_missing > 0.
if runs its block when the condition is True.
else runs its block when the condition is False.
Only one block ever runs - never both.

microLesson.headline: Gather evidence, then choose
paragraphs: The crab did not decide blindly. He watched what happened to the fish and looked for proof before choosing. A program does the same: gather information in variables, then ask a question.
If the condition is True, Python runs the lines under if. If it is False, it runs the lines under else. Only one path is taken.
You can combine conditions with and and or to make smarter decisions: if bones_visible and fish_missing > 0.
keyPoints: if condition: runs when the condition is True.
else: runs when the condition is False.
Combine checks with and / or for richer decisions.
Indent every line inside a block by 4 spaces.

challenge.title: The crab's decision
challenge.instruction: The crab sees fish bones near the heron's tree. If bones_visible is True, print "Snap the neck!". Otherwise print "Trust the heron". Write the if/else using the variable bones_visible.
challenge.starterCode:
# The crab sees bones near the heron's tree
bones_visible = True

# Should he trust the heron?
if bones_visible:
    print("Snap the neck!")
else:
    print("Trust the heron")
challenge.hint: bones_visible is True, so the if block runs.

check.message: The bones prove the heron is lying, so the crab fights back.

project.title: The Pond Watcher
project.brief: Help the crab count the fish. Start fish_count at 5. After each fish leaves with the heron, subtract 1. If fish_count drops to 2 or below, print "Time to escape!". Otherwise print "Still safe".
project.starterCode:
# The pond starts with five fish
fish_count = 5

# One fish leaves
fish_count = fish_count - 1

# Another fish leaves
fish_count = fish_count - 1

# Check if it is time to escape
if fish_count <= 2:
    print("Time to escape!")
else:
    print("Still safe")
project.successHint: Expected output: Still safe

check.message: 5 - 1 - 1 = 3 fish remain, which is above 2, so the crab stays safe for now.

title: The Brahmin and the Goat
moral: Listen to those who know, and let the rest pass by.
fable: A poor Brahmin received a fat goat as a gift and hoisted it onto his shoulders to carry home. Along the road he met a clever woman who cried, 'Brahmin! Why do you carry a dog on your shoulders? That is inauspicious!'

The Brahmin looked at the goat and said firmly, 'This is a goat, not a dog.' But a little farther on a man called out, 'Hey Brahmin, you are carrying a pig! Put it down before it dirties your clothes.' The Brahmin shook his head. 'It is a goat.'
Then a third person laughed and said, 'Fool, that is a donkey you are lugging about!' The Brahmin began to doubt himself. He set the goat down and stared at it, confused.

A wise old man walking by saw the trouble and said, 'Do not listen to every voice on the road. Ask yourself: what do you know it to be? If it looks like a goat, walks like a goat, and bleats like a goat, then it is a goat.' The Brahmin nodded, picked up his goat, and walked on.

riddle.question: The Brahmin hears three different claims about the animal on his shoulders. He must check each claim one by one and decide which is true. What Python idea matches this chain of checks?
options: A single assignment that never changes
A loop that repeats the same action
A chain of if / elif / else that checks each condition in turn
A list that stores many values
riddle.explanation: Each claim is a condition: is it a dog? a pig? a donkey? The Brahmin tests them one after another until one matches. In Python this is an if/elif/else chain - each elif checks a new possibility.

conceptReveal.title: elif: more than two branches
conceptReveal.summary: When a decision has more than two options, elif lets you check several conditions one after another. The first True branch runs; the rest are skipped.
points: elif adds extra branches between if and else.
Only the first True branch runs; the rest are skipped.
You can have as many elif branches as you need.
The else at the end catches anything that did not match.

microLesson.headline: Check one, then the next, then the next
paragraphs: The Brahmin does not decide after hearing the first voice. He listens to all three, checks each claim against what he knows, and only then makes up his mind. An if/elif/else chain works the same way.
if checks the first condition. If it is False, Python moves to the first elif and checks that. If that is also False, it tries the next elif, and so on.
The moment a condition is True, Python runs its block and skips the rest. The final else is a safety net for when none of the conditions match.
keyPoints: if / elif / else checks conditions in order.
Only the first matching branch runs.
Add as many elif branches as you need.
else catches everything the earlier branches missed.

challenge.title: What is on the Brahmin's shoulders?
challenge.instruction: The Brahmin meets three people, each claiming the animal is something different. Use an if/elif/else chain to check: if animal is "dog", print "Inauspicious!". If it is "pig", print "Dirty!". If it is "donkey", print "Foolish!". Otherwise print "It is a goat.".
challenge.hint: animal is "goat", which does not match any of the first three conditions, so the else block runs.

check.message: The animal is a goat, so none of the first three conditions match and the else block runs.

project.title: The Road of Voices
project.brief: Help the Brahmin check each claim. Write an if/elif/else chain: if claim is "dog" print "No!", elif claim is "pig" print "No!", elif claim is "donkey" print "No!", else print "Yes, it is a goat!". Try changing claim to test each branch.
project.successHint: Expected output: No!

check.message: The claim is "pig", which matches the second elif, so "No!" is printed.

title: The Great Monkey King
moral: Never ignore the signs of a changing world.
fable: A great monkey king led his troop of a hundred monkeys through a dangerous forest. One winter they found a mango grove beside a wide, still lake, and the monkey king tasted the fruit and declared it safe.

The troop gorged on sweet mangoes and fell asleep in the warm sun by the water's edge. But the monkey king stayed awake, watching the lake. He noticed the water creeping higher - warm snowmelt from the mountains was flowing in.
He shook his troop awake. 'The water is rising! We must move to higher ground at once!' But the monkeys were sleepy and full. 'Just a little longer,' they mumbled, and rolled over.

By morning the lake had swallowed the grove. Only the monkey king, clinging to the highest branch, survived. He wept for his friends and swore he would never again ignore the signs of a changing world.

riddle.question: The monkey king watches three things - the water level, the season, and whether his troop is awake - to decide what to do. What Python idea lets him check many conditions and choose the right action?
options: A single print statement
A variable that holds a number
An if / elif / else chain that checks each condition
A loop that runs forever
riddle.explanation: The monkey king gathers several facts and checks them in order: is the water rising? is it winter? is the troop sleeping? Each condition leads to a different action. An if/elif/else chain lets a program make exactly this kind of multi-condition decision.

conceptReveal.title: elif: many conditions, one choice
conceptReveal.summary: When the right action depends on several different facts, elif lets you test them in order and act on the first one that is true.
points: elif lets you test a second condition when the first was False.
Combine conditions with and: water_rising and season == "winter".
The first True branch runs; the rest are skipped.
You can chain as many elif branches as you need.

microLesson.headline: Read the signs, then decide
paragraphs: The monkey king does not act on a single fact. He watches the water, remembers the season, and notices his troop's state. Only when several signs point to danger does he decide to act.
An if/elif/else chain works the same way. The first condition is checked first; if it is False, the program moves to the next elif and checks that, and so on.
You can combine conditions with and and or to make smarter checks: if water_rising and season == 'winter' tests two facts at once.
keyPoints: elif tests a new condition when the previous one was False.
and combines two conditions: both must be True.
or lets either condition being True trigger the branch.
The first matching branch runs; the rest are skipped.

title: The Crow and the Snake
moral: When strength is not enough, let cleverness lead.
fable: A crow and her mate built a cosy nest in a great banyan tree. In a hollow at the foot of the same tree lived a black cobra, silent and greedy.

Every time the crow laid eggs, the cobra waited until the parents flew out, then slithered up and swallowed them. The heartbroken parents tried to guard the nest day and night, but they were far too weak to fight such a serpent.

So the mother crow studied the situation and chose a different move. One morning she snatched a golden chain from a queen bathing at the lake, then flew low and slow over the cobra's hollow with the servants chasing and shouting behind her.

Above the hole she let the chain drop in. 'Dig! The thief went into that hollow!' cried the servants, and as they dug, out came the snake - and they finished him at once. From that day the crows raised their chicks in peace.

riddle.question: The mother crow weighs three possible moves - guarding the nest, fighting the snake, or luring the humans - and picks the one that fits what she sees. What Python idea matches this kind of choice?
options: Repeating one action many times
Storing a value in a variable
Checking each situation in turn and acting on the first that fits
Printing the same message every time
riddle.explanation: The crow does not act blindly. She checks each possibility in order - can I win? should I guard? is a trick better? - and acts on the first situation that holds true. That is exactly how an if/elif/else chain chooses an action.

conceptReveal.title: Strategy: pick the action that fits
conceptReveal.summary: A program can weigh several situations and choose a matching action. The if/elif/else chain checks conditions in order and runs the first block that fits.
points: Each branch handles one situation: tree, hole, or away.
Python checks the branches top to bottom and runs only the first match.
The else block is the fallback when no condition fits.
Order matters - put the most specific check first.

microLesson.headline: Read the situation, choose the move
paragraphs: The mother crow never rushed. She looked at where the snake was, how strong she was, and what tools she had - then picked a plan to match. Programs do this with chains of conditions.
if tests the first situation. If it is False, elif tests the next one, and the next, until something fits. Only the matching block runs.
A good strategy lists its checks from most specific to most general, so the smartest plan is chosen before the fallback.
keyPoints: Check conditions from most specific to most general.
Only the first True branch runs; the rest are skipped.
else is the safe fallback plan.
Combine facts with and / or when a plan needs two things at once.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
fable: The hare laughed at the tortoise for being slow. 'Let us race,' said the tortoise calmly. 'I accept!' the hare chuckled, and they began.
In a flash the hare shot ahead. It grew so confident that it lay down under a tree for a nap, sure it would still win.
The tortoise did not hurry. It simply kept walking - step after step, lap after lap, never stopping, never giving up.
When the hare woke, the tortoise was already near the finish line. 'Slow and steady wins the race,' said the tortoise, and crossed first.

riddle.question: The tortoise wins by doing the same simple thing - walking - over and over in a steady rhythm. What is the pattern of its action?
options: One decision, then stop
The same step repeated many times in order
Storing a single growing number
Choosing between two friends
riddle.explanation: The tortoise repeats one action again and again. Python expresses repetition with a loop - for or while - so you never write the same line over and over.

conceptReveal.title: Loops: repeat without repeating yourself
conceptReveal.summary: A loop runs a block of code many times, so one line of code can do the work of a hundred.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
for lap in range(1, 6):
    print("Lap", lap, "- keep going!")
points: for runs the indented block once for each value.
range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (up to, but not including, 6).
while repeats as long as a condition stays True.
Loops keep code short and remove repetition errors.

microLesson.headline: Two loops, one idea
paragraphs: A for loop walks through a sequence - like a list of laps or a range of numbers - running its block once per item.
A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is True, just like the tortoise keeps walking until it reaches the finish line.
Whatever you repeat, the body (the indented lines) holds the action, and the loop header holds the pattern.
keyPoints: for x in range(...): repeats a fixed number of times.
while condition: repeats until the condition becomes False.
Always indent the body by 4 spaces.
Make sure while loops can end - no infinite walks!

title: The Banyan Deer
moral: One brave, kind choice can end a cycle of suffering.
fable: Long ago, two herds of deer grazed beside the fields of Benares - one led by the wise golden Banyan Deer, the other by the proud Branch Deer. The king of men, craving venison for his table, ordered hunters to snare the groves every single day.

So the two kings made a pact, and a quiet routine was born: each morning the lots were drawn, and whichever deer was chosen walked calmly to the killing block while the rest grazed in peace. Day after day the same ritual repeated, fair and orderly, like clockwork.

One morning the lot fell upon a pregnant doe of the Branch herd. She begged to wait until her fawn was born, but her own king refused. Without a word the Banyan Deer rose, walked to the block, and laid his golden neck upon it in her place.

The hunter dropped his knife in wonder. He freed the golden deer, then every deer he had caught, and told the king everything. Moved at last, the king decreed that no deer of the groves would ever be harmed again - and so the daily walk ended, never to repeat.

riddle.question: Every morning the herds drew lots, one chosen deer walked to the block, and the next morning the very same steps began again - until the day the king's decree changed everything. What Python idea matches this pattern?
options: Repeating the same routine again and again until a condition finally changes
Choosing between two different actions just once
Storing all the deer names in a single value
Printing one message and stopping immediately
riddle.explanation: The pact ran like a while loop: the same block of steps executed day after day while a condition held true ('the rule stands'), and it stopped only when something made that condition false.

conceptReveal.title: Repeat until the condition changes
conceptReveal.summary: A while loop performs the same block of steps again and again as long as its condition stays True. The moment the condition becomes False, the loop ends.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
rule_stands = True
day = 1

while rule_stands:
    print("Day", day, "- lots drawn")
    day = day + 1
    if day == 7:
        rule_stands = False
points: The condition is checked before every repetition.
If it is True, the whole block runs once more.
Something inside the loop must change - here, day grows until it hits 7.
When the condition turns False, the loop exits and the program continues.

microLesson.headline: Same routine, day after day
paragraphs: The herds' pact was a loop you could set your watch by: draw lots, chosen deer walks, everyone else rests. Nobody wrote those steps twice - the routine simply repeated.
In Python, a while loop keeps running its indented block while its condition remains True. It is perfect when you cannot know in advance how many repetitions you need.
But watch the exit: unless something inside the loop nudges the condition toward False - a counter growing, a flag flipping - the routine would run forever, like a pact no king ever ended.
keyPoints: while repeats as long as its condition is True.
for suits a known count; while suits 'repeat until something changes'.
Update a counter or flag inside the loop so it can end.
Code after the loop runs only once the loop has finished.

title: The Ant and the Dove
moral: Kindness given always finds its way back.
fable: A dove had built her nest on a branch that leaned over a cool stream. One parched afternoon, a little ant went down to the water to drink - and slipped in. The current gripped her at once, and every tiny kick only seemed to pull her further from the shore.

The dove saw the struggle and plucked a wide leaf, letting it fall right beside the drowning ant. Step by patient step the ant hauled herself up the leaf, rested as it drifted, and climbed off safely onto the muddy bank.

Days later the ant looked up to see a hunter below the dove's branch, aiming his sticky lime-twigs straight at her friend. The ant could not scare him away in one leap - so she began to climb: one step up his sandal, another up his ankle, again and again, until she reached his bare hand.
There she gave one sharp nibble! The hunter cried out and dropped his twigs, the dove heard the commotion and flew safely off - and the smallest of friends had returned the greatest of favours.

riddle.question: The drowning ant could not reach shore in one jump, and she could not climb the hunter in one hop - each rescue happened through small steps repeated until the goal was reached. What Python idea matches this?
options: Choosing between two actions just once
Storing a single value and never changing it
Repeating small steps over and over until the desired outcome is reached
Printing one message and stopping immediately
riddle.explanation: Both rescues ran like a loop: the same little step repeated, with progress counted each time, until the condition 'goal reached' finally became true and the loop ended.

conceptReveal.title: Repeat step by step until you arrive
conceptReveal.summary: A loop repeats the same small action, counting progress as it goes, and stops once the desired outcome is reached.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
step = 0

while step < 3:
    step = step + 1
    print("Step", step, "- closer to shore")

print("Safe!")
points: Each pass through the loop is one small step toward the goal.
The condition is checked before every repetition.
A counter grows inside the loop so it knows when to stop.
When the outcome is achieved, the loop ends and the program continues after it.

microLesson.headline: Little steps, repeated, get there
paragraphs: No single kick could carry the ant to shore, and no single hop could scale the hunter - but a step repeated is a journey. Loops turn tiny actions into great rescues.
In Python you set up a counter, check a condition, do one step of work, and let the loop wheel around again. Each pass brings the goal measurably closer.
The dove's kindness also worked this way: spot trouble, drop help, watch, repeat when needed. Programs are happiest doing exactly this kind of patient, watchful repetition.
keyPoints: Loops break big goals into many identical small steps.
while checks the goal condition before every pass.
Update the counter inside the loop or it never finishes.
Code after the loop runs once the outcome is achieved.

title: The Golden Goose
moral: Patience gathers gold; greed scatters it.
fable: Long ago the Bodhisatta lived as a goose whose feathers shone like beaten gold. Flying over a poor hut one day, he saw a widow and her two daughters struggling for their daily bread, and his heart filled with pity.

From that day a gentle routine began: each week the golden goose would return to the hut's roof and leave behind one single feather. The mother sold it at the market, and week after week, coin by coin, the little family climbed out of misery.

But comfort bred greed. 'Why wait for one feather at a time?' the mother grumbled. 'If I pluck them all today, tomorrow we shall be rich!' And when the goose came on his usual round, she seized him and stripped every feather from his body.

Yet feathers plucked in greed are not gold - they turned plain white as straw. The goose, unharmed and patient, waited until his wings grew strong again, then flew away, never passing that roof again. The weekly visits had ended, and no gold ever returned.

riddle.question: The goose's gift was not one event but a rhythm: every week he returned, every week one feather was sold, and the coins slowly grew. What Python idea matches a process that repeats once for each passing period of time?
options: Repeating the same action once for each period of time as it passes
Making one choice between two actions
Storing all the coins in a single value that never changes
Printing a message exactly once
riddle.explanation: The weekly visit is a loop where each pass stands for one period of time: the same small process runs again and again, and what it produces can be counted up as time goes by.

conceptReveal.title: Repetition across time
conceptReveal.summary: A loop can model a recurring process: each pass of the loop represents one tick of time, and values updated inside it accumulate as the weeks go by.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
coins = 0

for week in range(1, 5):
    print("Week", week, "- one feather sold")
    coins = coins + 1

print(coins, "coins gathered")
points: Each pass of the loop stands for one period of time - here, a week.
The body runs fresh every pass, just as the goose returns each visit.
A variable updated inside the loop accumulates what time adds up.
The loop ends when the planned span is finished - or when the pattern is broken.

microLesson.headline: Again and again, across time
paragraphs: One feather could never feed a family at once, but one feather every week could. Repetition over time is how small gifts become great fortunes - in stories and in programs alike.
Python loops walk through such schedules naturally: let the loop variable count weeks, run the same steps each pass, and keep totals in variables you update along the way.
Remember the mother's mistake too. A pattern that repeats only works while its condition holds - break the cycle too soon, or greedily force it, and the gold stops coming.
keyPoints: Use loops to repeat a process once per period of time.
range() acts like a calendar of planned repeats.
Accumulate results in a variable updated inside the loop.
The loop ends when its span finishes or its condition breaks.

title: The Monkey and the Wedge
moral: Don't tug at what you don't understand.
fable: A merchant's caravan halted in the forest at noon, and the woodcutters left a great log half split, its two halves held apart only by a wooden wedge. Nearby, a troop of monkeys came swinging down to play among the carts.

One young monkey could not take his eyes off that wedge. What a strange wooden tongue, he thought, keeping the mighty log open! He settled astride the log, gripped the wedge in both hands, and began to tug - gently at first, then harder.

Pull followed pull, each one loosening the wedge a little more, while the monkey checked again and again whether it still held firm. At last one mighty tug set it completely free - and the moment it slipped out, the heavy halves sprang shut with a snap.

The poor monkey's tail was caught fast beneath them. There he hung until the woodcutters returned, chattering lessons he would never forget: every pull had been his own, and the very last pull was the one that ended everything.

riddle.question: The monkey tugged again and again while the wedge held firm - and the instant it no longer held, the pulling stopped. Which Python statement works exactly this way?
options: A for loop that always runs a fixed number of times
A single if choice made once
A while loop: its block repeats while a condition is True, and stops the moment the condition becomes False
A variable declaration
riddle.explanation: while wedge_holds: keep pulling. Each pass re-tests the condition; when something inside the loop makes it False, the repetition ends right there.

conceptReveal.title: Repeat while it holds
conceptReveal.summary: A while loop tests its condition before every pass. While the condition is True the block repeats; when it turns False the loop stops instantly and the program moves on.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
wedge_holds = True
pulls = 0

while wedge_holds:
    pulls = pulls + 1
    print("Pull", pulls)
    if pulls == 3:
        wedge_holds = False

print("The loop has ended")
points: The stopping condition is checked before every single pass.
While it stays True, the whole block runs once more.
Something inside the loop must push the condition toward False.
The moment the test fails, Python jumps past the loop - no extra pass.

microLesson.headline: Every pull asks: does it still hold?
paragraphs: The monkey never decided to stop pulling - the wedge did. A while loop works the same way: you write the repeating action once, and the condition alone decides how many times it runs.
Before each pass Python asks the yes/no question. Yes means run the block again; No means leave the loop immediately and continue below it.
That is why loops need an ending built inside - a counter climbing, a flag flipping. Without one, the question never turns to No, and the monkey tugs forever.
keyPoints: while = 'keep doing this while the answer is True'.
The condition flips False through work done inside the loop.
Stopping conditions prevent infinite loops.
Statements after the loop run only once the condition has failed.

check.message: Four pulls while the flag held true, then the loop stopped exactly on cue.
