title: The Elephant and the Blind Men
moral: Put the pieces together to see the whole.
fable: In a village, six blind men heard that an elephant had arrived. They had never seen one, and each went to feel it with his hands.
The first touched the side and cried, 'It is a wall!' The second felt the tusk and said, 'No, it is a spear!' The third touched the ear: 'It is a fan!'
The fourth grasped the leg - 'It is a tree!' The fifth caught the tail - 'It is a rope!' The sixth touched the trunk - 'It is a snake!'
They argued loudly until a wise elder said, 'Each of you touched a different part. If you put your six ideas together, in order, you will begin to see the whole elephant.'

riddle.question: Each man's description is one piece of the elephant. How should the six descriptions be kept together so they can be looked at in order?
options: In a single number
In a collection that keeps items in order
In one yes/no choice
By making a decision
riddle.explanation: Six related values in a fixed order fit naturally in a list. Each position has an index, and you can grab any item by its position.

conceptReveal.title: Lists: ordered collections with positions
conceptReveal.summary: A list keeps many related values together in order, and you reach each one by its index.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
parts = ["wall", "spear", "fan", "tree", "rope", "snake"]
print(parts[0])   # wall   (first position)
print(parts[-1])  # snake  (last position)
points: Square brackets [ ] create a list; commas separate items.
Indices start at 0, so parts[0] is the first item.
Negative indices count from the end: parts[-1] is the last item.
len(parts) tells you how many items are in the list.

microLesson.headline: Positions, not names
paragraphs: A list is one variable that holds many values in a set order - like the six blind men's answers lined up in a row.
Each item has an index. The first item is at index 0, the second at 1, and so on. Python also lets you count backwards: parts[-1] is the last item.
You can change items, add new ones with append(), and loop over the whole list easily.
keyPoints: items = [a, b, c] creates a list.
First item: items[0]. Last item: items[-1].
len(items) gives the number of items.
Loop through with: for item in items:

challenge.title: The six views of the elephant
challenge.instruction: Store the six descriptions in a list, then print the first (index 0) and the last (index -1), one per line.
challenge.starterCode:
parts = ["wall", "spear", "fan", "tree", "rope", "snake"]

# Print the first and the last description
print(parts[0])
print(parts[-1])
challenge.hint: The first item is at index 0, the last at index -1.

check.message: The first view is 'wall' and the last view is 'snake'.

project.title: Elephant Notes
project.brief: Create a list called notes with three strings: "trunk", "tail", "tusk". Then print how many notes there are using len(), and print the last note.
project.starterCode:
notes = ["trunk", "tail", "tusk"]

# How many notes are there?
print(len(notes))

# What is the last note?
print(notes[-1])
project.successHint: Expected output: 3, then tusk

check.message: There are three notes, and the last one is 'tusk'.

title: The Crows and the Owls
moral: Wisdom can slip through any door.
fable: For years the crows and the owls were bitter enemies. From a hidden cave fortress the owl king swooped out night after night, and each morning the crow kingdom woke to find more names missing from its once-great flock.

So the crow council met. One minister said flee, another said make peace - and both plans were struck from the table. Only wise Meghavarna remained, offering a daring stratagem: let the flock attack him as a traitor and abandon him beside the owls' own cave.

Beaten and left for dead, he was found by the owl sentries - and soon the enemy's little band had a surprising new member. Inside the cave Meghavarna studied every passage, won the owl king's trust, and waited. One day he slipped out and returned carrying burning twigs in his beak.

Dropping the flames at the cave mouth, he sealed the owls inside their fortress forever. The crows rebuilt their flock feather by feather until every lost name was restored - proof that a kingdom, like any true collection, is defined not by staying the same but by how wisely it changes.

riddle.question: Through the whole war the crow kingdom kept its name, yet its contents never stopped changing - members were lost, a stranger joined the owls' cave, plans were added and struck off. What Python structure behaves like that?
options: A value fixed forever, which can never gain or lose anything
A collection that keeps its order while items are added, replaced, and removed
A single number counting the crows
One yes/no decision
riddle.explanation: Lists are collections whose contents can change: append() adds a member, index assignment replaces one, remove() takes one away - while the list itself keeps its identity and order.

conceptReveal.title: Lists that grow and shrink
conceptReveal.summary: A list is not a sealed box. Its contents can be added to, updated in place, and removed - while the same variable keeps holding the collection.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
flock = ["crow king", "scout"]
flock.append("Meghavarna")   # a new member joins
flock[1] = "decoy"           # an old role is replaced
flock.remove("decoy")       # a member departs
print(flock)
points: append() adds an item to the end of an existing list.
Assigning to an index updates one slot in place: flock[0] = "new name".
remove() deletes the first item that matches the given value.
The variable still points to the same list - only its contents changed.

microLesson.headline: A nest that changes, a name that stays
paragraphs: Night after night the crow kingdom changed - members fell, plans were dropped, an enemy slipped into the owl cave - yet everyone still called it the crow kingdom. One name, ever-changing contents.
Python lists work the same way. The variable keeps pointing at the collection while your calls reshape what is inside: append() welcomes newcomers, assignment swaps roles, remove() says farewell.
Collections like this are called mutable - changeable in place. It is exactly what made Meghavarna's trick possible: the owls assumed their group was fixed, but one careful addition undid them all.
keyPoints: Lists are mutable: their contents change without making a new list.
append() adds; remove() deletes the first matching item.
Index assignment updates a single slot: items[1] = "new".
len() always reports the current size, whatever just changed.

challenge.title: Choosing a Plan
challenge.instruction: The crow council starts with three plans: "flee", "make peace", and "the stratagem". Use remove() to strike off "flee", print the list, then strike off "make peace" and print again.
challenge.starterCode:
# Strike off the weak plans
council = ["flee", "make peace", "the stratagem"]

council.remove("flee")
print(council)

council.remove("make peace")
print(council)
challenge.hint: remove() deletes the first item equal to the value you pass in.

check.message: Two weak plans struck off - only the stratagem remains on the table.

project.title: Inside the Owl Cave
project.brief: Track how the owls' little band changes. Start with cave = ["owl king", "owl guards"]. Append "Meghavarna" and print the list. Then update the second slot with cave[1] = "trapped owls" and print again. Finally remove "trapped owls" and print one last time.
project.starterCode:
# The enemy's roster, reshaped by one visitor
cave = ["owl king", "owl guards"]

# A surprising new member joins
cave.append("Meghavarna")
print(cave)

# The fire changes everything
cave[1] = "trapped owls"
print(cave)

# And then they are gone
cave.remove("trapped owls")
print(cave)
project.successHint: Expected output: the list after appending, after updating, and after removing

check.message: Added, updated, removed - the cave's contents told the whole war.

title: The Dove, Crow, Mouse, Tortoise and Deer
moral: True friends are each other's strength.
fable: When a hunter's net swept down upon a flock of doves, their king Chitragriva gave a wise command: not one bird struggled alone. Flapping as one, the whole flock lifted the net into the sky and carried it to the mouse Hiranyaka, who gnawed every cord until all were free.

From that day a friendship grew - dove and mouse, then the crow Lightwing with his watchful eyes, then the deer with his swift hooves, and at last the tortoise, slow but steadfast. Five very different creatures, each with his own gift, bound together in one band.

When the deer stepped into a hunter's snare, the friends proved what a band can do: the crow circled high to keep watch, the deer held still while the mouse's sharp teeth worked strand after strand of the rope - each member called upon for exactly the help he alone could give.

And when the tortoise was carried off by hunters, the deer lay still pretending death while the crow pecked at him, drawing the hunter away - and the mouse chewed open the bag that held their friend. One by one, name by name, the five stood together against every snare.

riddle.question: Five very different friends - dove, crow, mouse, tortoise, deer - each needed by name, yet always kept together as one band. What Python structure keeps them together and lets you call on any one of them, or visit them all in turn?
options: Five separate variables that never meet
A single number counting the friends
A list holding all five, where each is reached by index and visited one by one in a loop
One yes/no decision
riddle.explanation: A list stores related characters together in order: friends[0] calls on the first directly, and a loop like 'for friend in friends:' visits every member in turn - exactly how the five friends worked.

conceptReveal.title: Friends in a row: lists meet loops
conceptReveal.summary: Lists hold many related values in order, indices reach any single element, and loops process every element - the three working best side by side.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
friends = ["dove", "crow", "mouse", "tortoise", "deer"]

print(friends[0])     # the first friend
print(friends[-1])    # the last friend

for friend in friends:   # visit every friend
    print(friend)
points: One list keeps all five related characters together, in order.
An index reaches one friend directly: friends[0] or friends[-1].
for friend in friends: visits each element without needing positions.
range(len(friends)) pairs each position number with its element.

microLesson.headline: Five names, one list, many rescues
paragraphs: Keeping five separate variables would be like five friends wandering the forest apart - easy to lose one, hard to gather them quickly. A list keeps the whole band in one place, in order.
Need one friend? Call by index: friends[2] brings the mouse. Need everyone? Let a loop walk the list from start to end, doing the same favour for each.
That pairing - store together, reach singly, process in bulk - is why lists and loops are inseparable companions in Python, just as the five friends were inseparable in the forest.
keyPoints: Related values belong together in one ordered list.
Index access reaches exactly one element: friends[i].
A for loop processes every element without repeating code.
range(len(items)) gives both the position and the element.

challenge.title: Roll Call of Friends
challenge.instruction: The five friends stand in order: "dove", "crow", "mouse", "tortoise", "deer". Store them in a list called friends. Then use range(len(friends)) to print each position and name on its own line, formatted like "0 - dove".
challenge.starterCode:
# The whole band, one by one
friends = ["dove", "crow", "mouse", "tortoise", "deer"]

for i in range(len(friends)):
    print(i, "-", friends[i])
challenge.hint: range(len(friends)) produces 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 - one position per friend; use friends[i] inside the loop.

check.message: Every friend called by position - the roll call runs itself.

project.title: Each Friend's Rescue Role
project.brief: In the great rescue, each friend had a part. Create two parallel lists: friends = ["dove", "crow", "mouse", "tortoise", "deer"] and roles = ["spots danger", "scouts the sky", "gnaws the ropes", "waits in water", "lures the hunters"]. Loop over the positions and print each pair on one line, separated by a space (for example: mouse gnaws the ropes).
project.starterCode:
# Every member has exactly one gift to give
friends = ["dove", "crow", "mouse", "tortoise", "deer"]
roles = ["spots danger", "scouts the sky", "gnaws the ropes", "waits in water", "lures the hunters"]

for i in range(len(friends)):
    print(friends[i], roles[i])
project.successHint: Expected output: five lines, each pairing a friend with their role

check.expected:
dove spots danger
crow scouts the sky
mouse gnaws the ropes
tortoise waits in water
deer lures the hunters
check.message: Two lists, one loop - each friend matched to the role only they could play.

title: The Elephant Caravan
moral: Wisdom walks in the right order.
fable: A merchant company preparing to cross the great wilderness sought out an ancient elephant as their guide, for he alone knew the desert's rhythm: rest through the burning day, march beneath the stars, and drink only at water holes tested in their proper turn.

The old elephant formed his column with care. The strongest young bull walked first, testing the path for soft sand and lions; behind him came the mothers with their calves, sheltered in the very middle of the line; and the mightiest elders closed the rear, trunks raised against every threat.

Not far behind travelled a second caravan, whose proud young leader scoffed at such ceremony. His elephants marched in whatever order they happened to start - calves straggling at the edges, no scout ahead - and at noon he led them straight to the first water hole without waiting, where lurking beasts lay in wait.

The wise column reached the far city whole and unharmed, every member exactly where wisdom had placed him. Same animals, same desert - but the caravan that honoured its order survived, while the one that scattered its sequence never arrived at all.

riddle.question: Both caravans had the same kinds of elephants, yet one arrived safely and one did not - because who marched first, middle, and last mattered more than anything else. What does this teach us about Python lists?
options: That lists scramble themselves to stay balanced
That a list keeps its items in an exact sequence, and processing follows that stored order
That every item in a list behaves identically wherever it sits
That order only matters for numbers
riddle.explanation: A list preserves position: index 0 truly comes first, and loops walk the sequence front to back. Reorder the same items and you get a different journey entirely.

conceptReveal.title: Order is information
conceptReveal.summary: Beyond its contents, a list carries meaning in the arrangement itself: the same items in a different order tell a different story.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
march = ["lead bull", "calves", "rear guard"]

print(march[0])     # the scout goes first
march.reverse()
print(march)        # now the calves march first - peril!

march.insert(1, "water master")
print(march)        # slotted exactly where needed
points: Lists keep items in the exact order they are placed.
The same items reordered make a different sequence with different results.
insert(position, item) adds an element at a chosen spot.
reverse() flips a list in place; loops always follow whatever order is stored.

microLesson.headline: Same members, different order, different fate
paragraphs: The wise caravan was not safer because it had different elephants - it was safer because each one stood in his right place. In ordered collections, position itself carries meaning.
Python lists remember sequence faithfully: whatever you append lands at the end, whatever you insert lands exactly where you aim it, and every loop visits elements front to back.
So before you process a list, ask the caravan leader's question: is this the right order? If not, tools like reverse(), sort(), and insert() can set the column straight before the journey begins.
keyPoints: Position matters: friends[0] and friends[-1] are different travellers.
insert(i, x) places an item precisely within the sequence.
reverse() and sort() change the stored order itself.
Loops process elements in stored order - fix the order before you loop.

challenge.title: Fix the Marching Order
challenge.instruction: The herd lines up, but the mothers with calves arrive late! Start with caravan = ["lead bull", "young bulls", "rear guard"]. Insert "mothers and calves" at index 1 so they march safely in the middle, then print the caravan.
challenge.starterCode:
# Everyone in their proper place
caravan = ["lead bull", "young bulls", "rear guard"]

caravan.insert(1, "mothers and calves")
print(caravan)
challenge.hint: insert(1, ...) slides everyone from index 1 onward one place back to make room.

check.message: The calves now travel shielded in the middle of the column.

project.title: The Safe Crossing
project.brief: Store the caravan's journey in order: route = ["test the water hole", "drink quickly", "cross the plain at night", "rest through the heat"]. Loop over the positions and print each as "Stage X - <step>" (X starting at 1). Afterwards print "First:" with route[0] and "Last:" with route[-1].
project.starterCode:
# The sequence is the survival plan
route = ["test the water hole", "drink quickly", "cross the plain at night", "rest through the heat"]

for i in range(len(route)):
    print("Stage", i + 1, "-", route[i])

print("First:", route[0])
print("Last:", route[-1])
project.successHint: Expected output: four numbered stages, then the First and Last lines

check.expected:
Stage 1 - test the water hole
Stage 2 - drink quickly
Stage 3 - cross the plain at night
Stage 4 - rest through the heat
First: test the water hole
Last: rest through the heat
check.message: Every stage in its stored order - that discipline carried the caravan through.

title: The Wise Quail
moral: Unity lifts what strength alone cannot.
fable: In a forest clearing a fowler spread his great net over the ground where quails came to feed, and day after day he gathered up whatever birds he had snared. At last the flock chose a wise quail as their king, and he taught them a single clever plan.

When the net fell, every quail was to slip her head through a mesh hole at once, then beat her wings together and rise as one. So it happened: net after net was lifted clean off the earth and carried away to a thorn bush while the fowler shook his empty hands.

But the flock grew careless in good fortune. One morning a feeding quail trod upon another's head, sharp words flew, and soon the whole company was split into squabbling singles, each sure she alone was right.

Down came the next net - and there was no rising together. Each bird struggled by herself, tangled deeper, and the fowler carried the entire quarrelling flock away in his basket, wondering how easily a band that soared as one had forgotten how to be counted together.

riddle.question: The wise quail never spoke of birds one by one - she always spoke of the flock: how many were present, and how each must act with all the rest. Which Python structure keeps a whole flock under one name, counts it, and visits every member?
options: One separate variable per bird
A single yes/no choice
A list holding the entire flock - counted with len() and visited with a loop
One large number
riddle.explanation: A list stores the whole group under one name: len(birds) tells you how many are present, and a for loop gives every bird her turn to act - just as the flock rose together.

conceptReveal.title: One flock, one list
conceptReveal.summary: Store a whole group in one list, measure it with len(), and let a loop give every member the same instruction.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
birds = ["quail1", "quail2", "quail3"]

print(len(birds))          # 3 - the flock, counted

for bird in birds:         # every bird takes part
    print(bird, "lifts the net")
points: One list keeps an entire group together under a single name.
len(birds) reports how many members are in the group right now.
for bird in birds: repeats the same action once per member.
Adding or losing members changes len() automatically - no recounting by hand.

microLesson.headline: Many wings, one name
paragraphs: No single quail was stronger than the net - but the flock was. Python lists work the same way: individual values become one group that you can command as a whole.
len() is your roll call, answering 'how many are with us?' at any instant. A loop is your command to march: every element receives the same instruction, one after another.
And remember the quarrel: the list itself never broke - the birds simply stopped acting like one collection. Keep your data grouped, and your group stays powerful.
keyPoints: Lists turn many values into one manageable group.
len() counts members instantly, however often they change.
Iteration gives every member the same turn.
Grouped data enables group actions - the heart of the quails' trick.

challenge.title: Count the Flock
challenge.instruction: Seven quails gather to feed: store them in a list called birds using the names "quail1" through "quail7". Print how many birds are in the flock using len().
challenge.starterCode:
# The whole flock, gathered in one place
birds = ["quail1", "quail2", "quail3", "quail4", "quail5", "quail6", "quail7"]

print(len(birds))
challenge.hint: len() takes the list inside its parentheses and returns the number of items.

check.message: Seven quails, counted instantly - the flock is ready.

project.title: Lift the Net Together
project.brief: Five quails face the falling net: start from birds = ["quail1", "quail2", "quail3", "quail4", "quail5"]. Loop over the flock and print each bird followed by "lifts the net" (separated by a space). After the loop, print how many flew using the pattern "<len> birds fly as one" - build it with len(birds), not a fixed number.
project.starterCode:
# Every wing beats as one
birds = ["quail1", "quail2", "quail3", "quail4", "quail5"]

for bird in birds:
    print(bird, "lifts the net")

print(len(birds), "birds fly as one")
project.successHint: Expected output: five 'lifts the net' lines, then '5 birds fly as one'

check.expected:
quail1 lifts the net
quail2 lifts the net
quail3 lifts the net
quail4 lifts the net
quail5 lifts the net
5 birds fly as one
check.message: Each bird did her part, and the flock rose as one - net and all.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
moral: Small helpers can do great work.
fable: A lion lay sleeping in the forest when a little mouse ran right over his nose and woke him. The lion caught the mouse and raised a paw to crush it.
'Please let me go,' squeaked the mouse. 'One day I may save you.' The lion laughed at such a tiny promise, but he let the mouse go.
Days later, hunters trapped the lion in a strong net. The lion's roars echoed through the forest, but no one came - no one except the little mouse.
The mouse gnawed the ropes, one by one, until the lion was free. 'You laughed at my size,' said the mouse, 'but small helpers can do great work.'

riddle.question: The mouse does one small, useful job - gnawing ropes to free a friend. If a friend got stuck tomorrow, the mouse would do the same job again. How could the lion 'ask' for that help each time without retelling the whole story?
options: With a reusable helper that takes a task and returns a result
By repeating one print statement many times
By making a single decision
By storing every word in one string
riddle.explanation: A function packages a useful action so it can be used again with different inputs. Give it what it needs, it does the job, and it returns the result.

conceptReveal.title: Functions: reusable helpers
conceptReveal.summary: A function is a named, reusable block of code. It takes inputs, does a job, and returns a result.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
def gnaw(ropes):
    freed = ropes - 1
    return freed

print(gnaw(3))  # 2
points: def names a function; its body runs only when the function is called.
Parameters receive the inputs: def gnaw(ropes).
return hands a result back to the caller.
Call it as many times as you like: gnaw(5), gnaw(2)...

microLesson.headline: Ask, work, return
paragraphs: A function is like the mouse's talent for gnawing: one action that can be reused whenever a friend is stuck. Define it once with def, then call it by name.
Inputs arrive as parameters - the values you pass in the parentheses. The body does the work, and return sends the result back out.
Once a function exists, the lion never needs the details again: just call gnaw(rope_count) and trust the helper.
keyPoints: def name(inputs): defines the function.
Parameters are placeholders for the inputs.
return gives the result back to the caller.
Call it with name(input) to use it.

challenge.title: The rope chewer
challenge.instruction: Finish the gnaw function so it returns ropes + 1 (the mouse chews one extra strand to be sure). Then call gnaw(3) and print the result.
challenge.starterCode:
def gnaw(ropes):
    return ropes + 1

# Call the helper and print the result
freed_ropes = gnaw(3)
print(freed_ropes)
challenge.hint: The function should return ropes + 1.

check.message: gnaw(3) returns 3 + 1 = 4, which is printed.

project.title: Lion's Rescue Kit
project.brief: Write a function rescue(ropes) that returns the message "Freed from N ropes!" using an f-string, where N is the number passed in. Then call rescue(5) and print it.
project.successHint: Expected output: Freed from 5 ropes!

check.message: The helper returns a message with the number of ropes.

title: The Tortoise and the Geese
moral: Silence can be the safest seat.
fable: When the lake where tortoise Kambugriva lived began to dry, his two dear goose friends offered to carry him through the sky to a water that never failed. He could not fly - but the geese knew one flight that worked for any traveller who trusted them.

Their plan was simple and reusable: a strong stick held between their beaks at both ends, and the passenger biting firmly onto the middle. One rule came with the ride - whatever you hear below, keep your mouth shut until you land.

Up they rose. Over a village below, folk pointed in wonder - 'Look! Two geese carrying a great wheel!' Kambugriva seethed. A wheel? He was a TORTOISE! The same flight that had carried him perfectly now ended in an instant: he opened his mouth to argue, lost his grip, and fell.

The geese flew on with heavy hearts, for their flight had never failed before. It had carried any quiet passenger over any distance; only its one condition had been broken - proof that even the finest reusable action depends on how it is used.

riddle.question: The geese's flight was one single plan that worked for any traveller - tortoise today, perhaps a mouse tomorrow - needing only the passenger's name filled in each time. What Python idea matches this?
options: Writing out the whole rescue again from scratch for every animal
A function defined once, whose parameter receives a different argument on every call
A value fixed forever inside one variable
A single yes/no decision
riddle.explanation: def carry(traveller): names the action once; the parameter traveller is a placeholder that each call fills in - carry('tortoise'), carry('mouse') - so one definition serves endless different inputs.

conceptReveal.title: Define once, fly many times
conceptReveal.summary: A function packages an action behind a name, with parameters as empty seats. Every call fills those seats with new arguments while the steps stay exactly the same.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
def carry_overhead(traveller):
    print(traveller, "bites the stick")
    print("The geese grip the ends and rise")

carry_overhead("the tortoise")
carry_overhead("the mouse")
points: def names the reusable action and lists its parameters.
Parameters are placeholders; arguments are the real values supplied per call.
Each call runs the identical steps with fresh inputs.
Change the definition once, and every future call benefits.

microLesson.headline: Same flight, different passenger
paragraphs: The geese did not invent a new way to travel for each friend - they owned one flight and welcomed whoever bit the stick. Functions give Python programs this same economy: write the action once, reuse it forever.
The parameter is the empty middle of the stick - carry_overhead(traveller) - waiting for whoever comes. Each call passes an argument, and the body runs with that value slotted into place.
And like the tortoise's one rule, functions come with expectations: pass sensible arguments, respect what the function assumes, and it will serve you faithfully call after call.
keyPoints: def packages an action behind a name for unlimited reuse.
Parameters are placeholders written at definition time.
Arguments are the actual inputs passed at call time.
One good definition can serve many different callers.

challenge.title: Board the Stick
challenge.instruction: Write a function carry(name) that prints "<name> bites the stick" (with name replaced by the input). Then call it once with "Kambugriva" and print nothing else.
challenge.starterCode:
# One flight, ready for any passenger
def carry(name):
    print(name, "bites the stick")

# The tortoise boards first
carry("Kambugriva")
challenge.hint: Inside the function, use the parameter name as if it were an ordinary variable; commas in print join pieces with spaces.

check.message: One definition, one call, one passenger safely aboard.

project.title: The Sky Ferry
project.brief: Turn the geese's flight into a reusable service. Write a function fly_with(passenger) that prints "The geese lift <passenger>". Call it three times - with "the tortoise", "the hare", and "the jackal" - then print "One action, many travellers" after all three flights.
project.starterCode:
# The reusable sky ferry
def fly_with(passenger):
    print("The geese lift", passenger)

fly_with("the tortoise")
fly_with("the hare")
fly_with("the jackal")

print("One action, many travellers")
project.successHint: Expected output: three lift lines, then the closing line

check.expected:
The geese lift the tortoise
The geese lift the hare
The geese lift the jackal
One action, many travellers
check.message: Three calls, three passengers, one unchanged definition.

title: The Ruru Deer
moral: Gratitude is worth more than gold.
fable: When great floods swept the river valley, a merchant found himself whirled downstream, crying for any help at all. From the forest came the golden deer Ruru, who plunged into the torrent, bore the struggling man upon his back, and set him safely on the bank.

The grateful merchant asked what reward he could give. 'Only this,' said Ruru, 'tell no one where I dwell, for kings hunt golden deer.' The man swore it and walked home - carrying with him the one payment the deer had asked.

Soon after, the queen dreamed of a deer who spoke with wisdom, and the king promised gold to anyone who could find such a wonder. The merchant heard the offer - and forgot everything the river had carried away. He led the huntsmen straight to Ruru's glade, pocketing his reward while the nets closed round.

But when the king beheld the golden deer, Ruru did not flee - he spoke. He told of the flood, of the rescue upon his back, and of the man whose greed outweighed his oath. Astonished by a deer who answered so wisely, the king lowered every weapon, spared the deer, and let his own judgement fall upon the faithless man instead.

riddle.question: Ruru took something in - a drowning man clinging to his back - and gave something back - a life set safe upon the shore; later he took the king's questions in and returned wise answers. What Python mechanism works exactly this way?
options: A variable that keeps only one value forever
A function that receives inputs through parameters and hands back a result with return
A loop that repeats without ever finishing
Two unrelated programs running apart
riddle.explanation: Parameters carry information INTO a function, its body works with them, and return sends a result back OUT - information in, useful answer out, ready for the caller to use.

conceptReveal.title: In through parameters, out through return
conceptReveal.summary: A function takes information in through its parameters, works with it, and sends a finished result back with return - a complete conversation between caller and helper.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
def rescue(traveller):
    return traveller + " is safe on the bank"

message = rescue("the merchant")
print(message)
points: Arguments supply the inputs; parameters receive them at call time.
The body treats parameters like ordinary variables while it works.
return hands exactly one result back to wherever the call was made.
A returned value can be stored in a variable, printed, or passed onward.

microLesson.headline: Questions in, answers out
paragraphs: Every rescue Ruru made followed one shape: someone came in over his back, and someone stepped out onto solid ground. Functions have the same shape - values arrive through parameters, a finished result departs through return.
The keyword return does more than end the function: it delivers the outcome to whoever called, so the answer can be stored in a variable, printed, or fed into another helper.
And because the result depends on the inputs, one definition can answer endless different calls - just as Ruru's wisdom fitted whatever question the king brought before him.
keyPoints: Inputs flow in as parameters; outcomes flow out via return.
return sends one value back and ends the call.
Store returned results in variables to reuse them.
Same definition, different arguments, fitting answers each time.

title: The Jackal and the Drum
moral: Investigation turns terror into understanding.
fable: A starving jackal wandered onto an old battlefield as evening fell - and froze. BOOM! A deep thunder rolled across the clearing again and again. Every hair on his back cried run, but hunger pinned him in place between fear and need.

So instead of bolting, he gave himself a method: watch first, creep second, touch last. From a safe distance he studied the sound until he saw its secret - a low branch, swinging in the wind, striking a great drum hung in a treetop.

Step by patient step he closed in while the boom rolled overhead. A paw tapped the drumhead: soft, slack, harmless. One quick tear and the 'monster' lay open - just hollow wood and stretched skin, with no demon inside, and beside it a fallen shield and enough food for days.

The jackal dined like a king that night, and carried away something greater than the meal: a method. Whatever thundered next - drum, storm, or shouting men - he could walk the same circle of watch, approach, test, conclude, and let the mystery explain itself.

riddle.question: The jackal did not invent a new plan for every frightening noise - he used one method each time: observe the clues, test a possibility, then conclude. What Python idea packages such a repeatable process?
options: Retyping every step from scratch for each new mystery
A function that wraps the whole procedure once, ready to be called with any new mystery
A single value stored forever
A choice made without looking
riddle.explanation: def investigate(mystery): stores the entire observe-test-conclude procedure under one name. Whenever a new mystery appears, one call hands it over as an argument and the familiar steps run again.

conceptReveal.title: A method you can call
conceptReveal.summary: Wrap a whole procedure - observing clues, testing, concluding - into a single named function, then reuse it on every new problem by passing the new subject as an argument.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
def investigate(mystery):
    print("Watching", mystery, "from cover")
    return "Explained: " + mystery

print(investigate("the booming drum"))
points: One def can hold an entire multi-step procedure.
The parameter names whatever subject the procedure studies this time.
Calling the function reruns the exact same steps on new material.
Returning the verdict lets the caller keep a record of each result.

microLesson.headline: Courage is a procedure
paragraphs: What saved the jackal was not bravery in general but a specific, repeatable sequence: watch, approach, test, conclude. Once discovered, that sequence could face any mystery the forest offered.
Programmers do the same with functions: the first hard problem teaches you a process; you wrap the process in a definition; after that, solving similar problems costs one short call each.
Notice the shape, too - information goes in (which mystery?) and a verdict comes out (what is it?). Procedures that take input and give output are the strongest kind to wrap in a function.
keyPoints: Procedures worth repeating belong inside a function.
Parameters carry the current case into the shared steps.
Return values hand back each investigation's conclusion.
Reuse turns yesterday's courage into today's routine.

title: The Sparrow and the Elephant
moral: Many small deeds can do what strength cannot.
fable: A sparrow pair had built their nest on a leafy branch beside the river, and there their eggs lay warm beneath them. One scorching afternoon a wild elephant, mad with heat, came crashing to the shade - and rammed the tree until the whole branch snapped, nest and eggs crushed beneath him.

The sparrow's mate wept over her broken home, but her tears turned to resolve. 'Strength is not mine,' she said, 'but friends are.' Word went out, and the helpers gathered: the woodpecker with his iron beak, the bee with her buzzing guile, and the old frog who knew every hollow of the shore.

'I will blind him,' said the woodpecker, and at noon he struck again and again at the giant's brow until dark rings ringed his eyes. 'I will lead him,' hummed the bee, circling closer and closer until the maddened elephant staggered after her sound, straight toward the lake.

There by the deep dry pit the frog waited, croaking from its very edge. Thirsty and half-blind, the elephant charged gladly at the watery song - and thundered down into the abyss. Each friend had given one small action; strung together, those actions had felled a giant.

riddle.question: No single friend could fight the elephant, yet the plan worked because each friend owned one clear action - blind, lure, croak - and the actions ran one after another. How does Python build big tasks this way?
options: By writing one enormous block of code that never changes
By breaking the big problem into small named functions - each doing one job - and calling them in order
By copying the same instructions everywhere by hand
By hoping the problem solves itself
riddle.explanation: Decomposition: split the giant task into small single-purpose functions - strike(), lure(), croak() - then call them in sequence so separate little actions combine into one grand plan.

conceptReveal.title: Small functions, one big plan
conceptReveal.summary: A large problem becomes manageable when each piece is wrapped in its own small function and a few lines call them in order - teamwork between definitions.
conceptReveal.codeExample:
def strike():
    print("The woodpecker blinds the giant")

def lure():
    print("The bee leads him toward the lake")

# The whole plan, three lines long
strike()
lure()
print("The frog croaks from the pit")
points: Give every helper its own small function with one clear job.
Names like strike() and lure() make the plan readable at a glance.
Calling functions in order runs the coordinated plan top to bottom.
Fix or improve one helper without rewriting the others.

microLesson.headline: Divide the giant
paragraphs: The sparrow could never push an elephant - so she never tried. She divided the impossible into possible pieces and handed each piece to a specialist. Programs grow the same way.
In Python, each piece becomes a function with a name that says what it does. The main plan shrinks to a short list of calls, reading almost like the story itself.
And like the friends, small functions stay independent: if the lure ever fails, you repair lure() alone while strike() keeps working. Division of labour is also division of risk.
keyPoints: Decompose: one big task, several small single-job functions.
Call the helpers in order to perform the full plan.
Well-named functions make plans self-explanatory.
Isolated functions are easier to fix, test, and reuse.
